The single item inside the labs folder (devnet-src)
A long listing with permissions, owner, size and date for each folder
The same ten folders in reverse alphabetical order
The long listing, but in reverse alphabetical order

The single item inside the labs folder (devnet-src)
A long listing with permissions, owner, size and date for each folder
The same ten folders in reverse alphabetical order

questions.explanation: Part 2, Step 2 (a-e). ls -lr shows options can be stacked: -l for the long format, -r to reverse the sort.

questions.text: How do you open the full manual page for a command, and how do you leave it again?
options: man [command], then press q to quit
help [command], then press Ctrl+C to quit
man [command], then press Ctrl+Z to quit
info [command], then press Esc to quit
questions.explanation: Part 2, Step 2f: man ls opens the manual (use Space to page through it), and q quits back to the prompt.

questions.text: What is the difference between ls --help and man ls?
options: --help only works for ls; man works for every command
--help prints a short summary of the options and returns to the prompt; man opens the full manual, which you must quit with q
They are the same command with different names
man is only for administrative commands, --help for everything else
questions.explanation: Part 2, Step 2f-g: man ls takes over the screen until you press q; --help just prints a shorter summary and hands the prompt straight back.

questions.text: What does the pwd command do?
options: Prints the current working directory, e.g. /home/devasc
Changes the current user's password
Prints the contents of the current directory
Prints the directory you were in before your last cd
questions.explanation: Part 2, Step 2h: pwd (print working directory) printed /home/devasc. It has nothing to do with passwords, despite the similar name.

questions.text: Fill in the command that jumps straight to the root of the file system, from anywhere.
questions.explanation: Part 2, Step 2j: cd / changed directly to /, confirmed with pwd.

questions.text: What does cd .. do?
options: Moves up exactly one directory level
Returns to the home directory, however deep you are
Returns to the root directory
Returns to whichever directory you were in previously
questions.explanation: Part 2, Step 2l: from ~/Documents, cd .. landed back in /home/devasc — one level up, not all the way home.

questions.text: cd documents (lowercase d) would work just as well as cd Documents.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: False. Part 2, Step 2k explicitly warns: "Remember that names are case-sensitive." Linux treats Documents and documents as different names.

questions.text: According to the lab's tip, which key auto-completes a directory name after you type its first few letters?
options: Enter
Tab
Ctrl+Space
Esc
questions.explanation: Part 2, Step 2k's tip: type the first few letters and press Tab to let the system finish the name for you.

questions.text: Why does sudo apt-get update need sudo in front of it?
options: It doesn't — the lab only adds sudo out of habit
Refreshing the system's package list is an administrative action that requires root privileges
sudo makes the command run faster
apt-get only exists as a root-owned alias
questions.explanation: Part 2, Step 3a: "This command will not work without using the sudo command" — refreshing package lists needs administrative access.

questions.text: What does the initial dash represent in -rwxr-xr-x?
options: The file type — here, a regular file
That the owner has no permissions at all
That the file is hidden
The number of hard links to the file
questions.explanation: Part 3, Step 1b (the lab's own first question). The first character identifies the file type; a dash means a plain file.

questions.text: What would be in the place of that first dash if the item were a directory instead of a file?
options: d
f
x
r
questions.explanation: Part 3, Step 1b. Compare with Step 2b's ls -l output from Part 2, where every folder line starts with d, e.g. drwxr-xr-x 2 devasc devasc 4096 ... Desktop.

questions.text: In the permission string -rwxr-xr-x, match each block of characters to who it governs.
allChoices: The file type (position 1)
The owner's permissions (positions 2-4)
The group's permissions (positions 5-7)
Everyone else's permissions (positions 8-10)

pairs.match: The file type (position 1)
The owner's permissions (positions 2-4)
The group's permissions (positions 5-7)
Everyone else's permissions (positions 8-10)

questions.explanation: Part 3, Step 1b's own questions, walking through the ten characters of -rwxr-xr-x left to right.

questions.text: Match each permission letter to what it grants.
allChoices: Permission to view the contents
Permission to modify the contents
Permission to run the file as a program

pairs.match: Permission to view the contents
Permission to modify the contents
Permission to run the file as a program

questions.explanation: Part 3, Step 1b's last three questions — read, write and execute.

questions.text: In -rwxr-xr-x 1 devasc devasc ... chromium_chromium.desktop, what does the first instance of devasc indicate?
options: The group that owns the file
The user who owns the file
The last user who edited it
The directory it lives in
questions.explanation: Part 3, Step 1b: the first name after the permission string and link count is the file's owning user.

questions.text: And what does the second instance of devasc indicate, in that same line?
options: The owning user, repeated for confirmation
The owning group
A symbolic link target
The parent directory's owner
questions.explanation: Part 3, Step 1b: the second name is the file's owning group.

questions.text: Fill in the operator that sends the output of echo into a brand-new file called myfile.sh, instead of printing it to the screen.
questions.explanation: Part 3, Step 2b: "the greater than (>) character redirects command output to a file."

questions.text: Why did ./myfile.sh fail with "Permission denied" right after it was created?
questions.context:
devasc@labvm:~/Documents$ ls -l myfile.sh
-rw-rw-r-- 1 devasc devasc 14 Apr 16 12:46 myfile.sh
options: The file didn't actually exist yet
None of the three permission groups include the execute (x) bit
Only root is allowed to run shell scripts
The script contained a syntax error
questions.explanation: Part 3, Step 2d-e: -rw-rw-r-- has no x anywhere, so nobody — not even the owner — is allowed to execute it yet.

questions.text: Fill in the command that grants execute permission on myfile.sh, fixing the "Permission denied" error.
questions.explanation: Part 3, Step 2f: chmod +x myfile.sh added the missing execute bit; Step 2g then ran the script successfully.

questions.text: After sudo chown root myfile.sh, the listing read -rwxrwxr-x 1 root devasc ... myfile.sh. What actually changed?
options: Both the owner and the group became root
The owning user became root, but the owning group stayed devasc
Only the permission bits changed; ownership stayed with devasc
The file was moved into root's home directory
questions.explanation: Part 3, Step 2h-i: chown without a group argument only changes the owning user. The second name in the listing, the group, remained devasc.

questions.text: Match each command used in Part 3 to what it does to a file.
allChoices: Creates a duplicate under a new name, leaving the original in place
Relocates the file, or renames it if the destination is in the same folder
Deletes the file outright
Adds execute permission so the file can be run
Transfers ownership of the file to another user

pairs.match: Creates a duplicate under a new name, leaving the original in place
Relocates the file, or renames it if the destination is in the same folder
Deletes the file outright
Adds execute permission so the file can be run
Transfers ownership of the file to another user

questions.explanation: Part 3, Steps 2-5, run in that order on myfile.sh/myfile_renamed.sh.

questions.text: In Part 3, mv myfile.sh myfile_renamed.sh renamed the file rather than moving it to a new location.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: True — Part 3, Step 3d. Since the destination has no path in front of it, mv just relabels the file in place.

questions.text: What is the key difference between > and >> when redirecting echo output to a file?
options: > appends to the file; >> overwrites it
> overwrites the file's existing contents; >> appends to the end of it
They behave identically; >> is just an older syntax
> writes to disk; >> writes only to memory
questions.explanation: Part 3, Step 6a-g: echo "Linux is POWERFUL!" > linux.txt erased the earlier "Linux is AWESOME!" line, while >> on linux2.txt left both lines intact.

questions.text: Fill in the operator that adds this line to the end of linux2.txt without erasing what's already there.
questions.explanation: Part 3, Step 6d: >> appends. A single > would have wiped out "Linux is AWESOME!".

questions.text: What does cat linux.txt > linux2.txt do?
options: Deletes linux.txt after copying it
Copies the contents of linux.txt into linux2.txt, leaving linux.txt untouched
Merges both files' contents into linux.txt
Renames linux.txt to linux2.txt
questions.explanation: Part 3, Step 6b-c: cat printed linux.txt's contents, and > redirected that output into linux2.txt. linux.txt itself was never modified.

questions.text: In the vi editor, which key returns you to Command mode from Edit mode?
options: i
a
Esc
questions.explanation: Part 3, Step 7b: i inserts at the cursor and a appends after it — both enter Edit mode. Esc is what brings you back to Command mode.

questions.text: Match each vi Command-mode action to what it does.
allChoices: Deletes (cuts) the current line
Yanks (copies) the current line
Puts (pastes) the yanked or deleted line
Writes (saves) the buffer to a named file
Quits the editor

pairs.match: Deletes (cuts) the current line
Yanks (copies) the current line
Puts (pastes) the yanked or deleted line
Writes (saves) the buffer to a named file
Quits the editor

questions.explanation: Part 3, Step 7b-c: "d will delete (cut), y will yank (copy), and p will put (paste)", then :w linux3.txt saved the edit under a new filename and :q exited.

questions.text: You can type :w and :q while still in Edit mode, without pressing Esc first.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: False. Part 3, Step 7c: you must be "in the command mode" before typing a colon to enter ex mode — Edit mode has no save/quit commands of its own.

questions.text: The grep command is case-sensitive by default.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: True — Part 4a: grep devasc /etc/passwd highlighted both lowercase instances of devasc but skipped the uppercase DEVASC in the same line.

questions.text: Running grep root /etc/passwd returned one line with three highlighted instances of "root". Where do those three instances come from?
options: The username field, the GECOS/comment field, and the home directory path
The username field, the UID, and the GID
Three separate matching lines in the file
The username field, repeated three times for emphasis
questions.explanation: Part 4b: reading the colon-separated fields left to right, "root" appears as the username, then again as the GECOS name, then again inside /root as the home directory — three hits in one line.

questions.text: Fill in the anchor character that makes grep return only lines where root is at the very start.
questions.explanation: Part 4c: the caret ^ anchors a match to the beginning of the line, so only the root:x:0:0... line qualified, not lines merely containing "root" elsewhere.

questions.text: What kind of lines does grep 'false$' /etc/passwd return?
options: Lines that start with "false"
Lines where "false" is the very last thing on the line
Lines containing the literal text "false$"
Every line that mentions "false" anywhere
questions.explanation: Part 4d: the dollar sign $ anchors to the end of the line, matching entries such as tss:...:/bin/false and lightdm:...:/bin/false.

questions.text: The lab runs grep 'd..m' /etc/passwd and both daemon and dnsmasq get highlighted. Why does dnsmasq qualify even though it's spelled differently from "daem"?
options: Each . matches exactly one character, so d..m also matches d + n + s + m in dnsmasq
grep ignores letter order by default
. matches zero or more characters, so it absorbed the extra letters
It's a coincidence — dnsmasq also contains the literal substring "d..m"
questions.explanation: Part 4e: the dot is a single-character wildcard, so d..m matches any 4-letter run starting with d and ending with m — daem(on) and dnsm(asq) both fit.

questions.text: What does grep '[8-9]' /etc/passwd return?
options: Lines containing an 8, a 9, or both
Only lines with exactly 8 or 9 characters
Lines containing the literal text "[8-9]"
Lines listing users with UID 8 or 9 specifically
questions.explanation: Part 4f: square brackets define a set/range to match against, so any line with an 8 or a 9 anywhere in it — like UID 38, 39, or 900 — was returned.

questions.text: What does grep '[,]' /etc/passwd return, and why?
options: Lines containing a literal comma — here, mostly the GECOS fields ending in ,,,
Lines with no commas at all, since brackets negate the character
Every line, since brackets are ignored by grep
Only lines with exactly one comma
questions.explanation: Part 4g: a single character inside brackets is matched literally, so this pulled every line whose comment field has commas, e.g. devasc:x:900:900:DEVASC,,,:/home/devasc:/bin/bash.

questions.text: The lab notes that grep 'new*' matches lines containing either "new" or "ne". Why does "ne" alone match?
options: * means zero or more of the character right before it, so the trailing w becomes optional
* is a wildcard for any single character
grep automatically ignores the last letter of any pattern
* makes the match case-insensitive
questions.explanation: Part 4h: * applies only to the w, and "zero copies" is a valid count — so the pattern really just means "an n then an e, optionally followed by more ws", matching things like nonexistent and network.

questions.text: Match each regular-expression symbol used in Part 4 to what it matches.
allChoices: The start of a line
The end of a line
Exactly one of any character
Any character within a set or range
Zero or more of the character immediately before it

pairs.match: The start of a line
The end of a line
Exactly one of any character
Any character within a set or range
Zero or more of the character immediately before it

questions.explanation: Part 4, Steps c through h, one symbol at a time.

questions.text: Match each shutdown variant used in Part 5, Step 1 to what it does.
allChoices: Halts the system immediately
Schedules a shutdown one minute out, broadcasting a message first
Cancels a shutdown that was already scheduled

pairs.match: Halts the system immediately
Schedules a shutdown one minute out, broadcasting a message first
Cancels a shutdown that was already scheduled

questions.explanation: Part 5, Step 1a and 1c. The lab is careful to have you cancel the scheduled shutdown so the VM stays up.

questions.text: The ip address output in Part 5 shows the dummy0 interface holding five separate IPv4 addresses (192.0.2.1 through 192.0.2.5). What does that demonstrate?
options: That five virtual interfaces are aliased as dummy0
That a single network interface can be assigned more than one IP address at once
That DHCP is cycling the interface through five addresses over time
That the addresses are misconfigured duplicates
questions.explanation: Part 5, Step 2a: one interface, dummy0, lists five inet lines — proof that an interface isn't limited to a single IP.

questions.text: In ping -c 4 192.168.1.1, what does -c 4 control?
options: It limits the ping to exactly 4 packets, then stops
It sets the packet size to 4 bytes
It waits 4 seconds before the first packet
It retries the ping 4 times if there's no reply
questions.explanation: Part 5, Step 2b: without -c, ping would keep sending packets indefinitely; -c 4 caps it at four, matching the four icmp_seq lines shown.

questions.text: Pinging www.cisco.com by name instead of by IP address triggers a DNS lookup before any ping packet is sent.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: True — Part 5, Step 2c: "Your VM will send out a DNS request first to get the IP address and then send the ping packets."

questions.text: What's the difference between plain ps and ps -e?
options: ps shows only the processes tied to the current terminal (like bash and ps itself); ps -e shows every process on the whole system
ps -e only shows processes owned by root
They are identical; -e just changes the column formatting
ps shows every process; -e narrows it to the current terminal
questions.explanation: Part 5, Step 3a-b: plain ps listed just bash and ps; ps -e listed dozens of system-wide processes starting from PID 1.

questions.text: In the ps -ef output, what is process ID 1?
options: kthreadd, the kernel's thread-spawning helper
/sbin/init, with PPID 0 — the root of the whole process tree
The current shell (bash)
Whatever process happened to start first after boot, which varies each run
questions.explanation: Part 5, Step 3d: root 1 0 0 20:57 ? 00:00:01 /sbin/init — PID 1, parent PID 0, the ancestor every other process traces back to.

questions.text: While paging through ps -e | more, what do the Enter key and the Space bar each do?
options: Enter advances one line at a time; Space advances a full screen at a time
Both advance a full screen at a time
Enter advances a full screen; Space advances one line
Enter quits more; Space advances one line
questions.explanation: Part 5, Step 3c: "the Enter key to display one line at a time, the space bar to display one screen at a time, or Ctrl+C to exit".

questions.text: Match each package-management command from Part 5, Step 4 to what it does.
allChoices: Refreshes the local list of packages available from the repositories
Searches the local package cache for a keyword to find the exact package name
Downloads and installs a specific named package and its dependencies
Updates every installed package and dependency on the system
Completely removes a package, freeing the disk space it used

pairs.match: Refreshes the local list of packages available from the repositories
Searches the local package cache for a keyword to find the exact package name
Downloads and installs a specific named package and its dependencies
Updates every installed package and dependency on the system
Completely removes a package, freeing the disk space it used

questions.explanation: Part 5, Step 4a-f, run in that order against the speedtest-cli package as an example.

questions.text: Of the commands used in Part 5, Step 4, which ones needed sudo to run? (Select four answers)
options: apt-get update
apt-cache search
apt-get install
speedtest-cli
apt-get upgrade
apt-get purge
questions.explanation: Every command in the lab that shows as devasc@labvm:~$ sudo apt-get ... needed elevated privileges — update, install, upgrade and purge. apt-cache search only reads the local cache, and speedtest-cli just runs a network test, so neither needs sudo.

questions.text: What does running passwd with no options prompt you for, in order?
options: Your username, then your new password
Your current password, then your new password, then a confirmation retype of the new password
Only a new password, typed once
A security question, then a new password
questions.explanation: Part 5, Step 5a: passwd asks for "Current password", "New password", then "Retype new password" before confirming the update.

questions.text: The lab asks you to interpret passwd -S's output. Match each field to what it means.
allChoices: The password is set and usable
The account can be re-passworded again immediately — no waiting period
The account never gets disabled for having an expired password

pairs.match: The password is set and usable
The account can be re-passworded again immediately — no waiting period
The account never gets disabled for having an expired password

questions.explanation: Part 5, Step 5b-c, using devasc P 04/17/2020 0 99999 7 -1: P is the password status, the first 0 is the minimum days before another change, and -1 is the number of days the account stays active after expiration — here, unlimited.

questions.text: The lab's own "Background / Scenario" note says this lab is meant to serve what purpose?
options: A substitute for prior Linux experience
A pass/fail gate before you may continue the course
A measure of your existing Linux skills, to help direct you to where you may need more review
A graded certification exam
questions.explanation: Background / Scenario: the lab "is not meant as a substitute for prior Linux experience" but "should serve as a good measure of your Linux skills and help direct you to where you may need more review."
